counting_note: Urdu has no classifiers — put the number straight before the noun. But the noun itself goes plural: ایک کتاب (one book), دو کتابیں (two books), تین روپے (three rupees). Exactly like Hindi.

culture.en: The Mughal fort-palace in Delhi — Friday prayers, peacocks, and the flag on Independence Day.
Lucknow's slow-cooked dum biryani and kebabs — dinner is an art form in Awadh.
The poetry gathering — ghazals and nazms recited live, the audience crying واہ واہ.
The night of Eid's moon — henna, sheer khurma, and greetings till late.
Urdu's beloved courtesy language — آپ, فرمائیے, تشریف رکھیے — politeness as poetry.

present_note: The present is stem + -تا (m) / -تی (f) + helper: ہوں (I), ہو (tum), ہیں (āp and they), ہے (is). So میں کھاتا ہوں (I eat, m), آپ کھاتے ہیں (you eat, respectful), وہ کھاتی ہے (she eats). Exactly like Hindi — only the script changed.

script_note: Urdu is written right to left in the beautiful Nastaliq style — start at the RIGHT end of the line! Letters change shape (start/middle/end) and join up, there are no capital letters, and short vowels (a/i/u) are usually left unwritten: you read مل as 'mil' (meet) or 'mal' by context. Dots do heavy lifting: ب ت ث ن ی are the same stroke with different dots. Persian gave Urdu پ چ ژ گ, India gave it ٹ ڈ ڑ, and nasalization comes from ں (nūn-ghunna): میں (main, I) vs مین — count the dots, then read.
